anchors.locator: Method › Study Sample, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 104); Results, 1st paragraph (p. 106); column heads of Tables 1 and 2 (p. 107)
Method › Measures, 3rd paragraph (p. 105); Method › Statistical Analysis (p. 106); References, Grant, Harford, Dawson, Chou & Pickering 1995 (p. 109)

claims.overstatement: One phrase overstates the source: 'conduct problems, other psychiatric disorders, family environment and other drug use were not measured'. This paper shows only that these were not used or adjusted for. The survey did measure other drug use: the AUDADIS reliability study it cites covered the alcohol and drug modules (p. 109, references), and the claim itself sends readers to the same survey's analysis of other drugs (Grant & Dawson, 1998). Suggested wording: 'were not taken into account in this analysis'. The rest of the claim's account of this source is accurate and appropriately hedged.
claims.note: Supported from this source: NLAES 1992, 42,862 adults interviewed once, about 92% of selected households and 97.4% of selected respondents (p. 104); 27,616 current (18,352) and former (9,264) drinkers (p. 106); the onset question excluded tastes or sips (p. 105); Table 1 Total column all 14 values with the three SEs quoted, read on the rendered page (40.6, 47.3, 40.8, 38.7, 30.6, 24.5, 16.6, 16.5, 11.4, 10.0, 9.5, 14.7, 13.6, 7.9); abuse without dependence 8.3–13.8% at 16 or younger, peak 13.8% at 14, 2.5% at 25 or older (Table 2); adjusted odds 14% and 8% lower per year with the six covariates as listed, and no ORs, CIs, p values or unadjusted estimates (pp. 106, 108); the editors' conversion to about 0.86 and 0.92 is right; the authors' description of onset age as a powerful predictor and of ages 16 and younger as a particularly vulnerable period (p. 108), and the closing paragraph's statement that the delay itself or, more likely, other associated factors may explain the link, with a call for a prospective study (p. 109). Inferences that are reasonable but not stated in the paper: 'often decades later' (respondents were 18 to over 65; the age distribution of drinkers is not given), and the exclusion of people who had died or were homeless (the paper says household sampling of the noninstitutionalized population of the contiguous US and DC). The point that two adjustments may follow from the disorder is supported by the definitions on pp. 105–106. One more point the claim could add: duration of drinking is age at interview (or last drink) minus age at onset, so adjusting for both age group and duration leaves the onset term partly tied to duration; the authors themselves say onset and duration still need to be disentangled (p. 109). No dosing or advice content in the claim. The paper's own suggestion to delay drinking until after 18 or 19 (pp. 108–109) is correctly left out of the claim.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 matches the card's design (meta-analysis), and critically low follows from items 9, 13 and 15, as the card says. Items 4, 7 and 15 fit an IPD consortium of population registries poorly; the substantive weakness is items 9 and 13: no appraisal of linkage or of cause-of-death certification and coding across eight countries and four decades. The rating should not be read as doubt about the counts and rates themselves.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is right: the first-week peak is supported, and the authors themselves state the 91.0% figure and the release-day artefact in the main text. One correction to results_show: 'Across 18 cohorts, crude death rates were highest on days 2-7' should say that the time-period analyses excluded two cohorts (see missed).

missed: Which cohorts the time-period figures rest on. Figure 2's caption (p. 1785) says Cunningham and King (New Zealand's only cohort) and Binswanger (Washington) could not provide deaths by day and were excluded from the time-period analyses, and the text ties the days 2-7 rate 1612 and the more-than-1-year rate 737 to Figure 2 (p. 1783). So the days 2-7, weekly and later-period rates, and the cause-specific rates by period (657, 135, 71), rest on 16 cohorts in seven countries. The release-day rate (4036) must come from cohorts with day-level data. KF 4 and KF 5 and the interpretation gap's 'Across 18 cohorts' should say so; only KF 6's note mentions the exclusion.

How the 4-week split in KF 7 was defined. The paper does not say whether 'more than 4 weeks after release' (14,671 of 16,126) counts from the index release or from the most recent release, or whether the release day is included. A rough check (my inference, approximate because pooled rates are not crude totals): the pooled poisoning rates for days 2-7 (657), week 2 (about 400, Figure 2B) and weeks 3-4 (about 265) imply roughly 420 such deaths in the first 4 weeks after the index release among 1.47 million people, against the 1,455 implied by the paper. So the count probably uses time since each release.

can_establish ('deaths in custody recorded as release-day deaths inflate day-1 estimates') and outcomes.validity_norms ('Inspection of the data showed ...') state the miscoding as shown. The paper hedges it: the data 'suggested' some cohorts 'might have' miscoded (p. 1781), the day-1 spike is 'probably at least partially an artefact' (p. 1784), and such deaths 'may have been' miscoded (p. 1786). The comparison 4036 against 826 also sets different cohort sets side by side, and 826 has an interval of 0-3455. KF 8 words it correctly.

Addition to RI 5: the 'other and ill-defined' subcategories in Table 2 (1121 + 2818 = 3939) also fall 3 short of their category total (3942). The non-communicable and injury subcategories add up exactly.

key_findings_flagged.correction: The review does not name DSM-IV: it says polysubstance dependence was diagnosed historically and refers to patients who 'previously met DSM Polysubstance Dependence criteria' (pp. 269-270). 'DSM-IV' is a correct gloss but should be marked as the editors', since the claim attributes it to the review. The rest (criteria, removal in DSM-5, severity continuum 2 to 11, population research recording frequency only) is confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; two domains high, so overall high. Self-citation count (8 of 71) re-counted.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: certain and causal wording from cross-sectional associations; 'clear' cognitive deficits beside null behavioural findings; no evidence cited for poorer treatment outcomes.

missed: The review states that in older groups people reporting polysubstance use in the past 12 months are very likely to report simultaneous use (ref. 22, p. 271, Prevalence section, 3rd paragraph), i.e. one national survey did measure same-occasion use; relevant to the claim that simultaneous use is hard to capture in surveys.

The annotation to ref. 22 gives the correlates as men, low education and high income (p. 274), while the text cites refs 21 and 22 for being single, low education and being employed (p. 271): a second text-annotation mismatch for ref. 22 besides 13.5% vs 13.2%.

The claim's cognition sentence drops ref. 62 (large differences on standard tests outside the scanner), which the card's key finding 11 correctly includes; the editor should align the claim with the card.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low: critical items 2, 4, 7, 9 and 11 not met. Item 9's note correctly says studies were appraised only as a gate for inclusion with no results reported, which is also why the claim's 'did not appraise' needs rewording. The card's baseline sum (21,370) recomputed.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. Recomputed ln2/0.091 = 7.6 and ln2/0.068 = 10.2 years.

missed: The treatment-at-baseline contrast (key finding 4) rests on the lifetime NESARC projection: by reconstruction from Fig. 4 the six cohorts without treatment at baseline are Moss 2010, Lopez-Quintero 2011, Trim 2013, Penick 2010, Vaillant 2003 and Galai 2003, and without Lopez-Quintero their standard rate is about 49%, below the treatment cohorts' 51% (editors' calculation; the review does not list the groups).

key_findings_flagged.correction: Table 1 (PDF p. 8) gives the forced-access period as 57 days of morphine HCl only 'with 4 choice days throughout', so 'morphine solution the only fluid for 57 days' should read 'the only fluid for 57 days apart from 4 choice days'. All statistics (18.6 vs 13.3 mg per rat; F = 200.9 df 1/69; F 26.38 df 1/23; F 7.26, 67.86, 36.44) confirmed. The abstinence result refers to the choice days after 2 and 5 weeks.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist; worst domain high (no search or criteria), so overall high is required and fits.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the summary paragraph overgeneralizes, the body and table qualify it.

missed: Table 1 prints df 1/69 for the Nichols-cycle housing and sex tests (F = 200.9 and 67.86) although at most 28 rats remained (df 1/23 elsewhere fits 27 rats in a 2 x 2 design); the error term therefore cannot be between rats, and the review does not say how the test was built (perhaps repeated days pooled). Cite the direction, not the size of F, as evidence of a housing effect.
Table 1's 1978 amounts (18.6 vs 13.3 mg morphine HCl per rat) carry no time base (per day or per period) and no body-weight correction; cite them 'as tabulated'.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Content and location confirmed, but the source is hedged: it says it is difficult to draw conclusions on MDMA from studies with non-user controls (p. 189), not that such comparisons cannot isolate its effects. Suggested: '...so comparisons with people who use no drugs make it difficult to draw conclusions about MDMA's effects.'

The source says some of the earlier investigations did not capture data on other drugs (p. 191, Summary 1st paragraph), not that earlier studies often did not. Replace 'often' with 'some earlier studies'. The rest is confirmed.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high (no systematic search); domain judgments reasonable.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the abstract's causal wording ('shown to contribute') against the body's 'inconsistent' (p. 190) is the main gap, and the card records it.

missed: The two wording slips above (KF0 'cannot isolate', KF10 'often') also appear in claim cl_gen_polydrug; correcting the card will help the claim follow the source's hedged wording.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high, driven by confounding, is right. Wording correction for the confounding note (and for cannot_establish and comparison.unmeasured_premorbid): other drug use, and possibly other psychopathology, were not used or adjusted for in this analysis. 'Not measured' is not supported: the AUDADIS reliability study cited on p. 109 covered drug modules, and the same survey's drug analysis is grant_1998 (already in the card's timeline). The polysubstance field's 'neither measured in this analysis nor adjusted for' is the accurate form.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the closing paragraph concedes that other factors more likely explain the link. Moderate would also be defensible: the Results' 'major contributor to the development' (p. 108) and the age thresholds for prevention read causation into a cross-sectional association.

missed: 'Not measured' versus 'not used' (see risk_of_bias note): p. 109 references show that the AUDADIS had drug modules; fix the three card fields that say other drug use was not measured.

pp. 105–106 with p. 109: for current drinkers, duration of drinking = age at interview minus onset age, so adjusting for age group and duration together leaves the per-year onset estimate conditional on duration and partly confounded with it, not a total association. The authors say onset and duration still need to be disentangled (p. 109). RI4 covers duration only as a possible consequence of the disorder.
p. 108: the comparison group for the abuse model (no disorder, or everyone without abuse including people with dependence) is not stated, so the 8% figure is hard to interpret; minor.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high, driven by confounding (no measures of conduct problems, psychopathology, family drug problems; a covariate that may follow the outcome). The other domain judgments are reasonable.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the authors' language of a powerful predictor and of the development of disorders, used for a cross-sectional, recalled-onset association of about 4-5% lower odds per year; the abstract reverses the two figures; the 40% applies only to people who used at least 12 times.

missed: Replication timeline: the paper does not say where Robins & Murphy (1967) was done; St. Louis and the 18-35 age range belong to Robins & Przybeck (1985) in the paper's text (p. 165). Minor.

'The only prospective study the authors cite' (replication, where it stands) is exact only for studies of age at first use and later drug problems: the paper also cites Kandel et al. (1986) and Bachman et al. (1985) on other consequences of adolescent drug use, without describing their designs (p. 164). The same phrase is in the claim.

The card's can_establish says people who started younger 'more often reported' a disorder; the disorders were DSM-IV diagnoses derived from the interview, so 'more often met criteria for' is more exact (same point as in the claim).

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high is right: the voucher comparison is completely confounded with period. Note for the editor: METHODS 5.3 reserves RoB 2 for laboratory studies with randomized or counterbalanced order, which this voucher comparison lacks (ROBINS-I would be the protocol's match for a non-randomized comparison of interventions); the overall judgment would be the most severe level either way.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: abstract generalization, untested $5.50 proportionality, and the abstinence extension.

missed: The vouchers were exchangeable for money or goods only at discharge (p. 88, Procedure, 2nd paragraph; p. 89, top), so the alternative was a delayed reward set against an immediate dose; the merchandise voucher was itself a voucher for a store voucher. This bears on how strong an alternative was tested and on the claim's phrase 'immediate rewards'.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: The reconstruction is confirmed independently. The consequence overstates the shrinkage: 0.66 is about 58% of the amount effect (1.13), a reduction of about two-fifths, not a halving. Suggested wording: 'which lowers the expectancy effect on amount in that study from about 1.1 to 0.66'.

risk_of_bias.note: AMSTAR 2 critically low; the six unmet critical items are right. One non-critical domain is generous: item 12 is 'yes', although item 9 judged the bias assessment inadequate, and only two features (deception quality, experimenter blindness) were tested against effect sizes. 'No' would be equally defensible and would not change the overall rating.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is defensible: the abstract calls the expectancy effects on deviant social behaviours strong at a mean g of 0.17, and 'no longer necessary' rests on counting non-significant interactions. But point (3) gives only one side. The authors themselves raise the confounded told-placebo/given-alcohol cell and argue on p. 358 that the effects were still separable. The gap text should say so (see missed).

missed: p. 358, left column, 3rd paragraph ('Success of the balanced-placebo design'): the authors accept that the design did not give an unconfounded manipulation of alcohol and expectancy, but argue that it still separated their effects. For no dependent variable in Tables 2-9 did alcohol and expectancy both have significant effects, let alone in the same direction, so they conclude the alcohol effects cannot be attributed to expectancy. This is the authors' answer to the 18-of-20 manipulation-check finding (key finding 16). It should sit beside that finding and in the interpretation gap, because claims citing the 18-of-20 figure (cl_alc_expectancy) draw the opposite inference without it.

Minor: cannot_establish says the review cannot speak to blood-alcohol levels at which a placebo deception cannot be kept up. That limit is the editors' general knowledge; the paper gives no doses and does not discuss it. Label it as the editors' point.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E very high for the causal (gateway) question; confounding very high and selection high are right. As a description of the order of first use the panel is well sampled, as the reasoning says.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One correction to the 'claimed' text: the running text is not only cautious. The body also calls marihuana a crucial step in the induction into illicit drug use, and a crucial stage before other illicit drugs (p. 913, left column, 8th paragraph). The causal-sounding wording and the caveats on p. 914 sit side by side in the body, not only abstract against text.

missed: p. 913, running text 8th paragraph: the 'crucial step' / 'crucial stage' wording is in the body as well as the abstract (see interpretation gap). The same correction applies to claim cl_gen_gateway, which contrasts the abstract with the text.

risk_of_bias.note: High overall is right: allocation by alternation, known to the staff, with the form in hand before people decided to take part, and 29% non-completion by unknown version. Recorded as design 'rct' with RoB 2, which judges a non-random sequence as high risk. Strictly, alternation makes this a quasi-randomized experiment, which Cochrane guidance also allows to be assessed as a non-randomized study (ROBINS-I). Either way the risk is high, and this evidence should not count as randomized when the claim's certainty is rated. 'Selection of the reported result' could reasonably be high rather than some concerns: the outcome scales were derived after data collection and the one-sided test is unstated. The overall judgment does not change.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right. The abstract's 'systematically different judgments' and the call for institutions to change terms rest on one of three post hoc subscales, with d about 0.17-0.18, two-sided p about .041 and alternating allocation; help-seeking, which the Conclusions invoke, was not measured.

missed: Minor: the Results present the four highest figures for 'perpetrator-punishment' (.69, .59, .53, .51, p. 205) as items 'most highly correlated' with the subscale, but they are the Promax pattern loadings of Table 1 rounded (.691, .586, .525, .506, p. 204), not item-subscale correlations. KF 7 repeats the figures correctly but calls them associations.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence, overall moderate: right for the weighted descriptions; the analytic telescoping statement is weaker, as the reasoning says.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial. One detail: 'among about 50 comparisons' (gap 3) and the outcomes field's '52 outcomes ... besides 11 sociodemographic characteristics' count outcomes, not tests: Tables 2–4 hold about 82 tests (two odds ratios per comorbidity row) and Table 1 compares 10 characteristics with 21 category contrasts (11 is the Methods list including gender).

missed: PDF p. 2, 2.2 Measures, 4th paragraph: 'onset of CUD' is not defined (first abuse or first dependence criterion set), and with abuse-only cases included the interval may end at a cannabis abuse diagnosis; worth stating in the operationalization alongside the unreported abuse/dependence split already noted.

Table 3 p-values fit a Wald F with about 65 design degrees of freedom (F 5.20 → p 0.0259); not an error, but it explains why an interval from the printed SEs is a little narrower than one from the printed F.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high: the co-twin design removes shared rearing and part of genetic confounding, but non-shared factors (peers, temperament) were not measured, fraternal pairs are pooled with identical pairs, and covariates were recalled at about 30 and chosen stepwise.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor is defensible because the authors themselves say strong causal conclusions cannot be drawn (p. 432) and hedge the mechanisms with 'may'. The weakest point is the abstract's statement that common genetic factors cannot solely explain the association, which rests on a non-significant zygosity interaction and unreported identical-pair estimates, with 50 identical discordant pairs not analysed; the title's 'escalation' and the closing call for interventions to prevent escalation (p. 432, last paragraph of the Comment) rest on lifetime prevalences without ages at progression.

missed: The concordance counts are internally inconsistent with the sample-flow figure: 229 concordant pairs (65 + 59 + 61 + 44) contribute 458 early starters and the 407 discordant pairs 407 more, i.e. 865 early starters among complete same-sex pairs (p. 430), but the whole interviewed sample had only 861 early starters (p. 428, Figure), before counting singletons and opposite-sex pairs. The concordance analysis and the analysed sample therefore cannot both be counted as printed; this strengthens reporting issue 2.

can_establish says the early starter more often reported 'later' alcohol dependence; the paper has no ages at onset of problems (p. 431 limitation), so for alcohol dependence (and abuse/dependence generally) only the lifetime difference, not its timing relative to early cannabis use, is shown. For other drug use, 'later' holds by construction because the 17 people who started another drug first were excluded.

key_findings_flagged.correction: Content confirmed. The point that participants may have cut down because intoxication would hurt their ratings (or to please the experimenter) is in the Discussion's 4th paragraph (p. 240, right column, the paragraph on loss of control), not the 3rd. The 3rd paragraph, which runs onto the right column, is the taste-discrimination alternative. The 5th-6th paragraph locators are right. Suggested locator: Discussion, 4th paragraph (p. 240, right column) and 5th-6th paragraphs (pp. 240-241).

risk_of_bias.note: RoB 2 some concerns overall, with the domain judgments as given. The experimenter's knowledge of the assignment is built into the deception (drinks mixed in front of the participant), and the volume outcome is objective, so the main expectancy effect is credible within the task.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The authors themselves name the limits that bound the claim (short task, low blood alcohol, taste-test demand). The unprinted simple-effect claim about the alcoholism group is correctly flagged. My reproduction of the editors' test is t(56) = 2.81, p = .007.

missed: p. 240, Discussion 3rd paragraph (left column end, continuing at the top of the right column): the authors say their data do not rule out a task explanation for the main finding. Men told the drinks held vodka may have sampled more because detecting vodka in a mixed drink is harder than judging tonic, which is a taste-discrimination effect rather than an expected-reinforcement effect. They argue against it because the alcoholism group drank more than social drinkers in the told-vodka cells, and because social drinkers sipped more often. Relevant data the card already has: the instructions did not change sip frequency (Table 2) but nearly doubled the amount per sip (Table 3), which fits larger gulps better than more tasting. Worth a key finding or a line in the interpretation gap, since it bears on what the expectancy effect means.

risk_of_bias.note: Editors' narrative-review checklist, overall high from the appraisal domain (no quality or bias assessment, p. 70). The card's calculations recompute: Table 1 median 14.8 with 28 of 37 below 30%; 24 of 27 studies before 2010.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor; the abstract's unquantified premise and the method-1 robustness statement against Table 1 are both on the cited pages.

missed: Provenance of the estimates: 71 of the 124 (57%) are the reviewers' own calculations, including the 2.7% minimum of the overall range. can_establish ('published estimates ... span 2.7% to 98.3%') and the design_detail should say so (Tables 1-3, pp. 64-66).

risk_of_bias.note: High overall on the editors' modelling checklist, mainly because no gateway model was fitted and the calibration targets only the margins. These concerns weigh on reading the model as the explanation of the data; they weigh much less on its narrower demonstration that the three phenomena can arise without any gateway effect, which is the only use the claim makes of it.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the statement that the phenomena can be explained completely (p. 1493) and the policy conclusion (p. 1503) go beyond a non-identification result, although the paper also says the gateway effect is not disproved and probably exists.

missed: The model results describe the relative risk as one for cases with and without earlier cannabis initiation (pp. 1499-1500), but the survey estimate it is compared with (24) counts cannabis use by 21 and hard-drug use by 21 regardless of order (p. 1499, Estimation of the relative risk effect); the two figures may not measure quite the same thing. Minor.

key_findings_flagged.correction: All F values and df confirmed at 300 dpi (32.6, 55.2, 11.7; 18.8, 80.98; 6.3, 11.4, 17.5). The last sentence should read 'no significant housing differences' in the 0.5, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml phases (Discussion, 2nd paragraph, p. 395): colony means were numerically higher at all three (Table 2) and no SDs are given. The Phase 3 mg/kg colony-over-isolated result is in Results, 3rd paragraph (p. 394), which the locator omits.

risk_of_bias.note: SYRCLE vocabulary; unblinded weighing by different methods in the two housings, the pole-climbing cost in Experiment 1 and unexplained missing rats justify the editors' overall high.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: the title and the genetic explanation are not tested, and Experiment 2 is called consistent with Experiment 1 despite reversed directions.

missed: The card's can_establish and interpretation_gap (results_show) say 'no differently' / 'no difference' at the lower concentrations in Experiment 1; the paper reports only that differences were not significant, with colony means numerically higher at all three.

Experiment 1's stated aim (p. 392, Introduction, 4th paragraph) was to test the computerized system's capability for data collection by comparing colony and isolated rats; the replication aim is stated later (p. 398).

The replication was close but not exact: Petrie used 4-day phases, 0.25 and 0.125 mg/ml and 0.05 mg/ml quinine (Table 1, p. 394), whereas Gage & Sumnall's Table 1 lists 5-day phases, 0.3 and 0.15 mg/ml and 0.06 mg/ml quinine for the 1981 study; Petrie does not describe the 1981 procedure or give its intake figures, so the 'up to seven times' and the comparison of isolated rats across studies cannot be checked from this paper.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence fits a descriptive comparison of women and men in one sample; overall high for the site's question is right (selection at treatment entry ties intervals ending at treatment to recruitment age; recalled ages; small effects absent in the youngest).

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial: 'relatively robust' and the advice to alert women in general go beyond small, age-confined effects in a treatment sample.

missed: p. 258, Discussion, 5th paragraph: the questionnaire did not ask ages at first drink or first intoxication, so this study cannot speak to time from first use to problems or treatment (the framing used by Piazza et al. and by the claim's opening sentence). Worth a key finding.

p. 256 with p. 253: 'first treatment' for the 735 is MATCH itself, but aftercare-arm participants were recruited from inpatient or day-hospital programmes, and how that index episode was counted is not stated; minor, affects which arm contributes to the 735.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI moderate is reasonable: random, nearly complete samples with blind interviewers, against self-reported and partly retrospective use, non-standard criteria, an unreported urine check after return and a short window. Recomputed Wilson intervals match the card within 0.2 points.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The abstract's 'essentially decreased to pre-Vietnam levels' against the rise in heavy use and injection (p. 959), and the causal turn on p. 960, are both on the pages cited.

missed: Treatment is reported in part, contrary to cannot_establish and the risk-of-bias reasoning ('treatment before or after return is not reported'): the departure urine screening was meant to detain men with positive urine for detoxification and treatment (p. 955, Introduction, 1st paragraph); the cohort was chosen for similar opportunities for treatment in the military (p. 955, Methods, 1st paragraph, continuing p. 956); Table 3 reports psychiatric treatment since return (26/12/6/12%, p. 960). What is not reported is drug treatment received per man or its relation to remission. The card should say that, and that the 134 men detected at departure 'because too addicted to quit' were the program's target.
The Results' convention that figures are for the general sample unless otherwise noted (p. 956, Results, 1st paragraph) bears on reporting issue 1 (the 95%).
Locator detail: the Methods' 1st paragraph (September 1971 chosen; similar treatment opportunities) starts on p. 955 and continues on p. 956; the card's recruitment field cites it as p. 956.

reporting_issues_flagged.note: PsycINFO's 10 records are confirmed (Fig. 1, p. 25), but the set logic is misdescribed (Table 1, p. 26). Sets #31 and #32 require a substance-use term plus the 'attitude of health personnel' term plus a care-delivery (#31) or stigma (#32) term. Set #30 needs no attitude term: it requires a health-personnel term, a substance-use term, and both a care-delivery and a stigma term. Correct statement: every retrieved record needed a care-delivery or stigma term (set #30 needed both), so attitude studies indexed without either were not retrieved. The consequence stated on the card stands.

risk_of_bias.note: Critically low follows from the unmet critical items 2, 4, 7 and 13, each borne out by the article. Item 9 at partial yes is generous but defensible: the Buckley checklist has confounding and subject-appropriateness items, yet every study passed and no per-study ratings are given. Item 1 at 'no' follows the project's convention for reviews without a comparator. Neither changes the overall judgment.

interpretation_gap.note: Substantial is right: the abstract's causal statements on consequences rest on two qualitative studies, and the review's text omits the one observational study with the opposite result. One wording fix in results_show: 'at least six papers' summaries ... moderate, neutral, appropriate or positive' should say five, plus one (Strauser et al.) with stigma below the criterion for negative stigma, matching the card's own KF 6.

missed: The '8 European countries' in Gilchrist et al. (2011) include Scotland (Table 4, p. 28: GR, ES, BG, IT, SI, SK, PL and Scotland). The card does not note this, and the claim derived from it says 'eight other European countries' alongside the UK; the countries outside the UK and Ireland are seven.

Minor: the design counts in 3.2 (20 quantitative, 5 interview or focus-group, 2 implicit association test, 2 observation) sum to 29 for 28 papers, so the categories overlap (for example, the implicit-association-test studies are also quantitative); KF 3 repeats them as if exclusive.

Minor: the two 'observation' studies are Segal and Dittrich (observed quality of care) and Curtis and Harrison (participant observation within a qualitative study). Only the first measured care delivered, which is how RI 1 rightly describes it.

risk_of_bias.note: Overall high follows from the no-search domain, as the editors' narrative-review checklist requires. One domain note needs a small correction: under Balance, the card says the critics' arguments (refs. 5, 90, 91, 97) are named but not set out; Box 4 (p. 260) does set out two of them (gene-environment correlation, larger maternal effects in MZ twins) and reports the lower meta-analytic estimate (ref. 98). The judgment 'some concerns' can stand because the review argues for the parameter's usefulness.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor. The card's results_show and claimed fields match the text (pp. 255, 256, 260, 263, 264).

missed: Box 4 (p. 260, 3rd paragraph) calls the view that a high heritability means a trait cannot be changed by intervention an incorrect perception. This supports the claim's 'environment cannot change it' sentence directly; the card covers it only through Box 2.
p. 258, Estimation of heritability, 4th paragraph: bias in a heritability estimate can come from assortative mating and selection (not in key finding 5).

p. 261, Heritability is not necessarily constant, 2nd paragraph: lower heritabilities in poorer environments are reported for morphometric traits but not for traits closer to fitness (a nuance to key findings 6 and 7).

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E overall high from confounding: neighbourhood is conditioned on but no individual propensity was measured.

interpretation_gap.note: Minor: the Discussion's talk of mechanisms and of a possibly causal association goes a step beyond associations located at two points of the sequence, but the abstract is hedged (the associations did not seem to arise solely from drug-seeking).

missed: The card's analysis field gives 'starting cocaine once offered, marijuana against none, 15 (11.3 to 19.8)'; the comparison group is people with no history of marijuana use whatever their alcohol or tobacco use (p. 923), not people who had used none of the three, so 'against no marijuana' is exact. The same wording is in the claim's magnitude.
